entities.name: Domitius Zenophilus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Domitius Zenophilus emerged as a prominent Roman senator and administrator during the early decades of the 4th century CE, distinguishing himself through an illustrious political career under the foundational reign of Emperor Constantine I. His tenure as consul in 333 CE, alongside his various provincial governorships and prefectural appointments, solidified his position within the Constantinian regime and offers a significant lens into the administrative machinery and elite power structures of the Late Roman Empire during a period of profound transformation.

Zenophilus's career trajectory underscores the opportunities available to skilled administrators within Constantine's consolidated empire. He served as proconsul of Africa, a crucial grain-producing province, before ascending to the prestigious and powerful position of Praetorian Prefect of the East. This latter role placed him at the apex of civil administration, overseeing vast territories, managing imperial finances, and administering justice across the eastern half of the empire. His consulship in 333 CE, shared with Flavius Optatus, marked him as a trusted pillar of the imperial establishment, participating in the highest ceremonial and administrative office of the Roman state.

His administrative actions contributed directly to the consolidation of Constantinian authority and the implementation of the emperor's policies across diverse regions, from North Africa to the eastern provinces. As praetorian prefect, Zenophilus would have played a critical role in fiscal management, military supply, and the maintenance of public order, thereby facilitating the stability that allowed Constantine's broader reforms, including the promotion of Christianity and the founding of Constantinople, to take root. His career reflects the growing professionalization and centralization of the imperial bureaucracy.
